analysis.one_liner: Lets federal K-12 education money follow each child to any public, private, or home school.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate education committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how federal money for elementary and secondary education is handed out. Instead of flowing to public school districts through programs like Title I and special education aid, the money would be divided evenly per child: public school students' share would go to their district, and students in private school or home school would get their share in an education savings account that parents could spend on tuition, tutoring, books, technology, therapies, or extracurriculars. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Families who want to leave public schools — including parents who home school and parents of children with disabilities seeking private placements or therapies — would get a federally funded account per child to spend on private tuition, tutoring, materials, and therapies [S3]. Families already paying for private school would get a subsidy on top. Private schools and education vendors (tutoring, online materials, testing, diagnostics) would gain a large new customer base of publicly funded accounts [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families leaving public schools; private schools

how_it_helps.text: It lets federal K-12 money under Titles I, III, IV, V, and VI of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act follow a child to a public school, private school, or home school, whether the child is learning in person or remotely.

Children in private school or home school would receive their share through an education savings account that parents could spend on tuition, tutoring, books, technology, testing fees, therapies, or extracurriculars.
It extends the same arrangement to special education money under the IDEA, letting a child with a disability take their share to a private school or home school, including for educational therapies.
It states that nothing in the bill would cut off a child's eligibility for free or reduced-price school lunch, and that money must supplement, not replace, state and local education funds.

analysis.who_pays: Public school districts would lose federal dollars for each child enrolled in private or home school, even though public schools have fixed costs and must serve every child who enrolls — students remaining in public schools would be spread across a smaller federal share [S3]. The quality of private and home school education receiving the money would be largely unregulated, since the bill bars federal or state control over non-public providers [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Public schools and their remaining students

drawbacks.text: Federal money that previously went only to public school systems would be divided with private and home schools, shrinking the per-student funding base of public schools, which must accept and educate every child who shows up.

Private schools and home schools receiving the money would face no federal or state control over curriculum, hiring, or standards, since the bill expressly bars such control — families would have to judge quality themselves.

The bill would channel public education money through individually managed education savings accounts, adding administrative machinery and leaving low-income families with less help navigating the choices than wealthier families.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real for families who want out of their assigned school — especially ones who could never afford private tuition — and for parents of children with disabilities seeking therapies. But the cost is borne by the public school system itself: every child who leaves takes federal money with them, while public schools still have fixed costs (buildings, teachers) and remain the only schools required to take every child. The bill's anti-supplanting language does not stop that dynamic. Whether it helps or hurts low-income children overall depends on contested evidence about how voucher programs perform, and the bill did no committee work that could have tested that.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, sent to the Senate education committee, and never heard from again; no hearing, no vote, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill's entire action history is two steps: it was introduced on March 10, 2021, and read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
No further action was taken for the rest of the Congress, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
It attracted only one cosponsor, so it never had the support base that pushes a bill onto a committee's agenda.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public school systems keep the federal funding formula untouched, and the committee that would have had to weigh the tradeoffs never had to take a position.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-led Senate never took the bill up.

industries.note: Federal Title I, IDEA, and related funds would be divided per child, so public districts lose dollars for every student enrolled elsewhere while still bearing fixed costs and the obligation to educate everyone. Districts serving the poorest students would feel it first.

Private schools would gain a new revenue stream — federal per-student money paying tuition — with no federal or state control over non-public education providers. Private school access becomes the official channel for some public education funds.

industries.industry: Tutoring, online learning, and education technology providers
industries.note: The allowable uses include tutoring, online materials, and diagnostic tools, creating a new federally funded customer base for these vendors.
Homeschoolers would gain access to federal per-student funds for materials, a long-sought benefit for some families, with few strings attached.
